claims.text: Rapid quenching produces a highly randomized, disordered atomic configuration in Co–Cr–Fe–Ni nanoparticles.
Slow cooling produces pre-existing short-range order in Co–Cr–Fe–Ni nanoparticles.
Highly disordered nanoparticles have higher activation barriers for atomic diffusion than nanoparticles with pre-existing short-range order.
Higher atomic-diffusion activation barriers increase resistance to thermally induced segregation and phase separation.
Cooling-rate variation can create Co–Cr–Fe–Ni nanoparticle batches that differ primarily in their degree of local chemical order.
The initial degree of local chemical order influences atomic-diffusion kinetics and the activation energy for elemental migration.
The activation energy for elemental migration controls the onset of phase segregation.
The enhanced configurational entropy of the rapidly quenched, nearly random solid solution raises the activation barrier for atomic diffusion.
Kinetic freezing in the rapidly quenched state retards the formation of nucleated ordered clusters during thermal exposure.
Nucleated ordered clusters can serve as seeds for progressive elemental segregation under prolonged thermal exposure.
After identical thermal aging, rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain more nearly equiatomic elemental distributions and exhibit less segregation than slowly cooled nanoparticles.
Slowly cooled nanoparticles will exhibit measurable elemental segregation and phase separation after thermal aging.
Synchrotron XRD and pair-distribution-function analysis can verify the predicted differences in elemental distribution and segregation.
Pre-existing short-range order in slowly cooled nanoparticles is associated with lower diffusion activation energy and faster segregation under thermal stress.
The proposed disorder-controlled mechanism is expected to operate in inert atmospheres over 473–1923 K, including the 773–1173 K catalytic range.
Strongly oxidizing or reactive atmospheres may produce behavior different from that predicted under inert conditions.
